meta.subtitle: The first 72 hours without power, network, or outside help

cover.title: Gotowi72
cover.subtitle: Household crisis-preparedness planner
cover.footer: Based on official guidance from Poland's RCB, Germany's BBK, and Sweden's MSB

intro.heading: Why 72 hours?
paragraphs: The governments of Sweden, Germany, and a growing number of Central and Eastern European countries now explicitly recommend that citizens be able to survive the first 72 hours of any crisis on their own — a power grid failure, a flood, a cyberattack on infrastructure, or a border incident — before emergency services and state aid are fully mobilized.

This isn't a movie scenario. It's the same standard that Sweden has followed for years (the "If Crisis or War Comes" brochure), that Germany's BBK guide teaches, and that Poland's Government Centre for Security (RCB) has been actively promoting since 2025/2026.

This planner turns those recommendations into a concrete, checkable list — no doom-mongering, no conspiracy theories. It's the same logic as a fire extinguisher in the kitchen: you hope you never need it.
intro.sources_note: Sources and full figures — see the last page.

categories.title: Water
categories.note: At least 3 liters per person per day (drinking + cooking + basic hygiene) — Poland's RCB recommendation. Germany's BBK states 1.5 l for drinking + 0.5 l for cooking as an absolute minimum.
items: 9 liters of bottled water per person (3 days x 3 l) — in small, portable 1.5 l bottles
Extra water for hygiene and flushing, if you have storage space
Water purification tablets or a travel filter as a backup plan
A container per person to refill in case of evacuation

categories.title: Food
categories.note: Items that don't need a fridge, cooking, or use minimal water/energy to prepare.
items: Whole-grain pasta, groats, rice (note: many need cooking — keep no-cook options too)
Canned legumes (chickpeas, beans, lentils)
Canned vegetables, fruit, meat, fish
Dried fruit and nuts
Honey, jam, oils — long-shelf-life staples
Dark chocolate and muesli bars — quick energy
Long-life crackers / bread
Ready-to-eat food that needs no heating, in case power/gas is out
Pet food and water for at least 3 days

categories.title: Medicine and first aid
categories.note: The first thing people forget in a panic — and the hardest to replace during a crisis.
items: A supply of any regular medication (at least 3–7 days, ideally more)
A complete first-aid kit (bandages, plasters, antiseptic, scissors, gloves)
Pain and fever relievers, activated charcoal, anti-diarrheal medicine
A written list of your prescriptions and dosages (in case you need a different pharmacy)
Potassium iodide tablets — only per current guidance from local authorities; never self-dose preventively
Face masks, hand sanitizer

categories.title: Cash
categories.note: Card terminals and ATMs stop working during a power or network outage. The Netherlands recommends about €70 per adult and €30 per child for 3 days; Sweden about 2,000 SEK per person for a week.
items: Cash in small denominations (10–50 in your local currency) — as a starting point, aim for the equivalent of roughly 3 days' worth per adult
Kept at home, not only in your bank account — accounts can become temporarily inaccessible
Part of it somewhere safe but quickly reachable — not in a safe whose key is at the office

categories.title: Communication, light, power
categories.note: When mobile networks and the internet go down, a battery radio is the one reliable way to receive official announcements.
items: A flashlight per person + spare batteries
A battery- or crank-powered radio with FM/DAB+ reception
A high-capacity power bank (ideally solar-rechargeable)
Candles + matches/lighter (used carefully, only with ventilation)
A charging cable for every device in the house
A list of important phone numbers written on paper, not just saved in a phone

categories.title: Documents and hygiene
categories.note: Keep copies in a waterproof pouch; originals stay in a safe place at home.
items: Copies of ID cards, passports, property deeds, insurance policies
A backup of key data (document photos in the cloud and offline on a USB drive)
Hygiene items: soap, toothpaste and toothbrushes, toilet paper, wet wipes
Trash bags and disposable gloves — endlessly useful in a crisis
Extra hygiene and baby/child supplies, if applicable

family_plan.heading: Family communication plan
family_plan.intro: Mobile networks and the internet are usually among the first things to fail during a power outage or a deliberate attack on infrastructure. This plan needs to be agreed BEFORE a crisis — there's no time to work it out once one starts.

sections.title: 1. Meeting point
points: Agree on a spot at home or nearby where the family will regroup if a crisis catches everyone in different places (e.g., outside the building, outside school)
Agree on a second, backup meeting point further away (e.g., a relative's place in another part of town), in case evacuation becomes necessary

sections.title: 2. An out-of-area contact person
points: Choose one person outside your city/region as the central point of contact — local calls often fail while long-distance calls still get through
Every household member should know their number by heart and have it written on paper, not just saved in a phone

sections.title: 3. Who does what
points: Decide in advance who grabs the first-aid kit, who grabs the documents, who's responsible for the kids, who's responsible for pets
Children should know the basics: who to call, where to go, if they get separated from a parent

sections.title: 4. Communication without a network
points: A battery radio for official announcements (national/local civil protection authorities)
Agree on a simple note or sign left at home (e.g., on the door) in case you get separated with no way to communicate
Consider PMR walkie-talkies as backup short-range family communication

sections.title: 5. People who need extra help
points: Plan ahead for elderly, ill, or disabled family members and neighbors
Write down their needs (medication, equipment, mobility) somewhere the whole family can access

grab_bag.heading: "15 minutes to leave the house" — the evacuation bag
grab_bag.intro: If you're told to evacuate immediately, you won't have time to look for things. Pack this in advance, keep it in one place near the door, and check the contents every six months.

categories.title: Documents and money
items: ID cards / passports (or copies in a waterproof pouch)
Cash in small denominations
Payment cards
A copy of insurance policies and property/rental documents
A written list of important phone numbers

categories.title: Health
items: Medication for at least 3–5 days + a dosage list
A mini first-aid kit
Spare glasses/contact lenses, if applicable

categories.title: Gear
items: A power bank + a cable for every phone
A headlamp + batteries
A pocket knife / multitool
A battery radio (if you haven't already grabbed the household one)

categories.title: Clothing and protection
items: A change of clothes per person, suited to the weather
Sturdy shoes (kept by the door, not on a top shelf)
A rain poncho / warm jacket
An emergency thermal blanket per person

categories.title: Food and water
items: A bottle of water per person + a way to refill it
Energy bars / dried fruit for one day per person

categories.title: For kids and pets
items: A small favorite toy or comfort item for a child
Diapers/formula, if applicable
A leash, food, and the pet's health record

categories.title: Keys
items: Spare house and car keys
The key/tool to manually shut off gas or water, if needed

variant_apartment.heading: Version: Apartment
variant_apartment.intro: In an apartment building, what matters most is storage space and what happens when the elevator and central heating stop working.

adaptations.title: Storing supplies
adaptations.text: Use the space under the bed, on top of wardrobes, and in closets — flat, stackable containers for water and food take up less room than large jugs.

adaptations.title: The elevator and stairwell
adaptations.text: During a power outage the elevator won't work — plan whether you can carry supplies or help elderly residents down the stairwell. Keep a headlamp by the door for this.

adaptations.title: Backup heating
adaptations.text: Without a stove or fireplace, backup heating options are limited — stock warm blankets, low-comfort-rating sleeping bags, and layered thermal clothing instead of open-flame heaters (carbon monoxide risk in a sealed apartment).

adaptations.title: Shutoff valves and meters
adaptations.text: Find out now where the main gas and water shutoffs are in your apartment or building basement, and how to close them safely.

adaptations.title: Building meeting point
adaptations.text: Agree on a meeting point outside the building with your neighbors — in dense housing it's easy to get separated during an evacuation.

variant_house.heading: Version: House with a garden
variant_house.intro: More space means you can hold a bigger stockpile, but also more things outdoors that need securing.

adaptations.title: Storing supplies
adaptations.text: A garage, basement, or shed lets you keep a 7–10 day supply instead of just 72 hours — consider a rotating "buy a bit extra every shopping trip" system.

adaptations.title: An extra water source
adaptations.text: A rainwater tank, a well, or large containers in the garage filled ahead of time are a real advantage over an apartment — keep purification tablets on hand if the water isn't drinkable straight from the source.

adaptations.title: Backup heating and power
adaptations.text: A wood stove or fireplace plus a stock of firewood is a solid backup heating plan. If you have a generator, store fuel according to regulations (outdoors, away from ignition sources) and never run it inside an enclosed space.

adaptations.title: Securing the garden and property
adaptations.text: Ahead of an expected weather threat, secure garden furniture, trampolines, and tools — in an infrastructure crisis these can also become dangerous flying debris.

adaptations.title: Your car as a resource
adaptations.text: Keep the fuel tank at least half full — a car is a backup source of phone charging, radio, and warmth in an extreme situation.

adaptations.title: Livestock
adaptations.text: If you keep chickens, goats, or other animals, plan at least 14 days of feed and water for them, plus a backup plan in case you need to leave.

sources.heading: Sources
items: Sweden — Myndigheten för samhällsskydd och beredskap (MSB), "If Crisis or War Comes" brochure (2024)
Germany — Bundesamt für Bevölkerungsschutz und Katastrophenhilfe (BBK), "Ratgeber für Notfallvorsorge und richtiges Handeln in Notsituationen"
Poland — Government Centre for Security (RCB), 72-hour supply recommendations
The Netherlands and Sweden — central bank recommendations on household cash reserves
sources.disclaimer: This planner is for general, educational purposes. For topics such as potassium iodide tablets, evacuation orders, or medical assistance, always follow current guidance from your local authorities and emergency services.
